subsection: 4. Serbia, the Second International and the outbreak of war in 1914

notes.h: The Balkan setting: a power vacuum and two rival empires
notes.b: To see why a quarrel with a small state could start a world war, you first need the setting. The Ottoman Empire was losing control of the Balkans, and two larger empires wanted to fill the gap.
points: The Eastern Question was the problem of what would happen as Ottoman power in the Balkans declined. The decline left a vacuum, so Austria-Hungary and Russia both wanted to fill it and became rivals.

Austria-Hungary was a multinational empire of Germans, Hungarians, Czechs, Poles, South Slavs and others. Any nationalist movement therefore threatened its survival, because each nationality could claim the right to leave.
Pan-Slavism was the idea that Russia, the largest Slav and Orthodox Christian power, should protect and lead the Slavs of the Balkans. This gave Russia a reason to take Serbia's side.

By 1907 Europe was split into two blocs: the Triple Alliance of 1882 (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and the Triple Entente (Britain, France, Russia). A Balkan quarrel could therefore draw in several Great Powers.
Russia was weakened by defeat in the Russo-Japanese War (1904-05) and by the revolution of 1905. This is why it was less able to stand up to Austria-Hungary and Germany in the crises that followed.
notes.tip: Key concepts here are nationalism and balance of power. Use nationalism for the South Slav and Serbian movement that threatened Austria-Hungary, and balance of power for each side's fear of losing status.

notes.b: Serbia was a young state whose independence was won through the Great Powers, and it stayed economically tied to its larger neighbour. Its nationalism soon pulled against that tie.
points: The Congress of Berlin (1878, the Balkan settlement, not the African Berlin Conference of 1884-85) recognised Serbia's full independence from the Ottoman Empire and gave it extra territory.
At the same Congress Austria-Hungary was given the right to occupy and administer Bosnia-Herzegovina, which stayed under nominal Ottoman rule. This set up the later crisis over Bosnia.

Serbia became a kingdom in 1882 under Milan Obrenović. It was a client of Austria-Hungary (dependent on it and under its influence), whose market took Serbia's main exports of pigs and other livestock.

Serbian nationalists, like other South Slav nationalists, dreamed of uniting the South Slavs (Serbs, Croats, Slovenes and the Slavs of Bosnia) in one state. This is why Serbia and Austria-Hungary were bound to clash.

Millions of South Slavs lived inside Austria-Hungary, so a strong Serbia that attracted them threatened to break up the empire. Vienna saw Serbian nationalism as a danger to its survival, not just a foreign matter.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the Congress of Berlin (1878, Balkans) with the Berlin Conference (1884-85, Africa). For a 30-mark Serbia paragraph, give the dates 1878 and 1882 and explain why the South Slav aim threatened Austria-Hungary.

notes.h: Serbia as a fulcrum of Great Power rivalry
notes.b: A fulcrum is the pivot a lever turns on. After 1903 Serbia turned from Vienna to Russia, and from then on its disputes with Austria-Hungary pulled the bigger powers in behind it.
points: In June 1903 army officers murdered King Alexander Obrenović and Queen Draga in Belgrade; Dragutin Dimitrijević (Apis) was one of the conspirators. Peter I of the Karadjordjević dynasty became king. Sources differ on the day, so give the month only.
The new regime turned away from Vienna and towards Russia and France. The Obrenović dynasty had been pro-Austrian; the Karadjordjević dynasty was pro-Russian.

Russia saw itself as protector of the Balkan Slavs and wanted to stop Austria-Hungary dominating the Balkans. It also wanted its warships to be able to pass through the Straits (the Bosporus and Dardanelles).

The Pig War began in 1906, when Austria-Hungary closed its border to Serbian livestock. It wanted to punish Serbia for a customs agreement with Bulgaria (1905) and for ordering artillery from France rather than from Austria-Hungary.
Serbia found other markets, so the Austrian economic hold weakened and Serbia became less dependent on Vienna. Sources disagree on when the Pig War ended, so give no end date.

Franz Conrad von Hötzendorf, Chief of the Austro-Hungarian General Staff from 1906 (briefly removed 1911-12), repeatedly urged preventive war against Serbia. His fear was that a strong Serbia could encourage the empire's Slav nationalities to leave.
Serbia was a fulcrum because a small state's quarrel with Austria-Hungary drew in Russia, its protector, and through the alliances Germany (behind Austria-Hungary) and France (behind Russia).
notes.tip: Examiners reward the cause-and-result link from Serbia to 1914. Give the reasons for the Pig War as the Bulgarian customs agreement and the French guns. Do not say it was about Serbia's trade links with France.

notes.b: In 1908 Austria-Hungary turned its occupation of Bosnia into outright annexation. This humiliated Russia and Serbia, who both resolved not to back down again.
points: Austria-Hungary had occupied and administered Bosnia-Herzegovina since 1878, though it remained under nominal Ottoman rule. The Young Turk revolution of July 1908 in the Ottoman Empire raised the chance that Bosnia would be reclaimed, so Austria acted.

In September 1908 the Austrian foreign minister, Count Aehrenthal, met the Russian foreign minister, Izvolsky, at Buchlau in Moravia. They discussed a swap: Austria would annex Bosnia, and Russia would gain support for opening the Straits to its warships.
Austria announced the annexation on 6 October 1908, before Russia had won anything on the Straits, so Russia felt cheated. Bulgaria declared full independence at the same time.

Serbia regarded Bosnia as having a large Serb population, so it was outraged. It protested, prepared for war and demanded compensation. The Narodna Odbrana (National Defence), a nationalist society, was founded in 1908 in reaction to the annexation.

In March 1909 Germany demanded that Russia accept the annexation and drop its support for Serbia. Russia, still weak after the war with Japan and the revolution of 1905, gave way, and Serbia formally accepted it that month.
The crisis humiliated Russia and Serbia and left both determined not to back down again. Russia accelerated its rearmament, and Austria-Hungary and Germany drew closer.
Germany's backing of Austria-Hungary in the Balkans set a precedent, which is why it mattered again in July 1914.
notes.tip: Know one cause, the events in order, the outcome and the effect on later crises. The effect to give is that Russia and Serbia vowed not to back down again. Do not say Serbia mobilised in 1908-09.

notes.b: The Balkan states used the Ottomans' weakness to grab land, and then fought over the spoils. Serbia emerged much bigger, which alarmed Austria-Hungary.
points: In 1912 the Balkan League was formed by Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece and Montenegro, with Russian encouragement. Italy's war for Libya (1911-12) had exposed Ottoman weakness, so the League struck.
The First Balkan War began in October 1912 and was ended by the Treaty of London in May 1913. The League defeated the Ottomans, who lost most of their European lands.

A conference of ambassadors met in London in 1912-13 under Sir Edward Grey, the British Foreign Secretary. It created an independent Albania, backed by Austria-Hungary and Italy, which denied Serbia the Adriatic port it wanted.

The League then quarrelled over the spoils. In the Second Balkan War (June to August 1913) Bulgaria attacked Serbia and Greece and was beaten, with Romania and the Ottomans joining against it. The Treaty of Bucharest followed in August 1913.
Over the two wars Serbia almost doubled its territory, gaining Kosovo (in the First Balkan War) and much of Macedonia (confirmed at Bucharest).

In October 1913 an Austro-Hungarian ultimatum forced Serbia to withdraw its troops from Albania, and Serbia complied. A stronger Serbia, backed by Russia and unsatisfied over the Adriatic, alarmed Austria-Hungary further, and Conrad pressed for war.
Conference diplomacy had contained the wars, but Austria-Hungary concluded that next time it must fight. Russia's prestige now depended on Serbia, so it too would find it hard to give way.
notes.tip: Say Serbia almost doubled over the two wars. Do not say Bucharest gave Serbia Kosovo, because Kosovo is not part of Macedonia and was taken earlier. Do not mix up the three Londons: the 1839 treaty, the 1912-13 conference and the May 1913 treaty.

notes.h: The Black Hand and the assassination at Sarajevo
notes.b: Serbian nationalism now had a violent wing. Officers in Serbia armed young Bosnians, and one of them killed the heir to the Habsburg throne.
points: The Black Hand (official name Unification or Death) was a secret society founded in May 1911 by Serbian army officers. Its leader was Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević, known as Apis, head of Serbian military intelligence by 1914. It aimed at a Greater Serbia.
Young Bosnia was a movement of young South Slav nationalists in Bosnia, mostly Bosnian Serbs. They were armed and trained with Black Hand help because both wanted to end Habsburg rule.
Do not confuse the groups. The Black Hand was a secret society of officers (1911), the Narodna Odbrana was a public nationalist society (1908), and Young Bosnia was Princip's group of Bosnian youths.

Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Habsburg throne, visited Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 after army manoeuvres. That day is Vidovdan (St Vitus's Day), the anniversary of the Serbian defeat by the Ottomans at Kosovo in 1389.

In the morning Nedeljko Čabrinović threw a bomb that missed the Archduke's car. Later the car took a wrong turn and stopped near Gavrilo Princip, who shot Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg. Both died.
The assassins were arrested. Princip, born in 1894, was 19, so he was under 20 and could not be executed. He was sentenced to 20 years and died of tuberculosis in prison in 1918.
The conspirators' pistols and bombs came from Serbia via the Black Hand. How much the Serbian government, headed by Prime Minister Nikola Pašić, knew of the plot is disputed.

Austria-Hungary decided to use the murder to crush Serbia, but first sought Germany's backing. Count Berchtold was the foreign minister, while Count Tisza, the Hungarian Prime Minister, at first opposed war. Count Hoyos was sent to Berlin on 5 July 1914.
notes.tip: Examiners credit correct dates. Give 28 June 1914, the failed bomb, the wrong turn and Princip. Say the weapons came from Serbia but that the government's knowledge is disputed.

notes.h: The July crisis, 1914: from blank cheque to war on Serbia
notes.b: In the five weeks after Sarajevo each step made the next harder to avoid. First Austria-Hungary secured German support, then it set Serbia terms designed to be refused.
points: On 5 July Wilhelm II promised Austria-Hungary support, and on 6 July Chancellor Theobald von Bethmann Hollweg confirmed it. This 'blank cheque' was unconditional support in whatever action it took against Serbia. Berlin hoped for a short, localised war.
French President Raymond Poincaré and Prime Minister René Viviani visited St Petersburg from 20 to 23 July 1914. This reaffirmed French support for Russia, which encouraged Russia to stand by Serbia.

On 23 July Austria-Hungary delivered an ultimatum (a final demand with a deadline) to Serbia: ten demands and a 48-hour deadline. They included the suppression of anti-Austrian propaganda and organisations, and Austrian officials to take part in the inquiry inside Serbia. It was meant to be refused.

On 25 July Serbia accepted most demands but refused Austrian officials a part in the judicial inquiry on Serbian soil. Serbia began mobilising the same day, and Austria-Hungary broke off relations that day.

On 26 July Grey proposed a conference, but Germany declined. The Tsar and Kaiser also exchanged the 'Willy-Nicky' telegrams in late July, but mediation failed. Sazonov was the Russian foreign minister.
Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914, three days after breaking off relations, and Belgrade was shelled from 29 July.
notes.tip: A tight paragraph from Sarajevo to 4 August with correct dates earns marks. Do not run together the breaking of relations (25 July) and the declaration of war (28 July). Show how each link led to the next.

notes.h: The July crisis: mobilisations, the Schlieffen Plan and Britain's entry
notes.b: Once Austria-Hungary was at war with Serbia, the alliances and military timetables turned a Balkan war into a European one within a week.
points: Russia ordered partial mobilisation (against Austria-Hungary only) on 29 July and general mobilisation on 30 July. Germany demanded on 31 July that Russia stop, and treated general mobilisation as a cause of war.
Germany and France ordered general mobilisation on 1 August. Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August, and Austria-Hungary declared war on Russia on 6 August.

Alfred von Schlieffen, German Chief of the General Staff until 1906, drew up the Schlieffen Plan and Helmuth von Moltke the Younger modified it in 1914. It aimed to defeat France in about six weeks through Belgium before Russia was fully mobilised, then turn east.
This is why Russian mobilisation meant war in the west. Germany had to strike France first and could not wait, so it would attack through Belgium whether or not France was the aggressor.
Germany sent Belgium an ultimatum on 2 August and Belgium refused on 3 August. Germany declared war on France on 3 August and invaded Belgium on 4 August.

Britain was a guarantor of Belgian neutrality under the Treaty of London of 1839 and used the invasion of Belgium as its reason. It was also concerned for the balance of power and had the Entente with France. Its ultimatum to Germany expired at 11 pm on 4 August 1914.

Bethmann Hollweg called the 1839 treaty 'a scrap of paper' to the British ambassador, Sir Edward Goschen, on 4 August 1914. Britain's entry made it a European war and, through the empires, a world war.
Italy declared neutrality in early August 1914 because the Triple Alliance was defensive and Austria-Hungary had not consulted it. It entered the war on the Entente side in 1915.
notes.tip: Examiners want how each link led to the next: blank cheque, ultimatum, Russian mobilisation, Schlieffen Plan, Belgium, British entry. Do not say Britain was bound by the 1839 treaty, because historians dispute that. Say it was a guarantor and give its other reasons.

notes.h: The Second International: founding, parties and divisions
notes.b: The Second International was a federation of socialist and labour parties. Its members believed that workers had more in common across borders than with their own ruling classes, and it looked strong on paper before 1914.
points: Marxism holds that society is divided by class struggle and that workers of all countries share interests. Its aim is to replace capitalism with socialism. The SPD (the Social Democratic Party of Germany) was Germany's Marxist party.

The Second International was founded in Paris in July 1889, the centenary of the French Revolution, as a federation of socialist and labour parties. It had a permanent International Socialist Bureau in Brussels from 1900. It believed in workers' solidarity across borders.

The German SPD was the largest and most respected party. In the 1912 Reichstag election it won 110 seats and became the biggest party. Other members were French socialists under Jean Jaurès, British Labour, and Russian and Polish Marxists such as Lenin and Luxemburg.

Its parties were divided over reform or revolution. Eduard Bernstein, an SPD revisionist, wanted socialism by gradual reform, while revolutionary Marxists such as Luxemburg and Lenin rejected this. August Bebel led the SPD until his death in 1913.
They also disagreed over how to stop a war. Jaurès and Keir Hardie supported a general strike against war, but the SPD leaders opposed making it binding.

The Stuttgart Congress (1907) resolved that socialists should do everything to prevent war and, if it broke out, to work to end it quickly and use the crisis to hasten the fall of capitalism. The last part came from an amendment by Luxemburg, Lenin and Martov.
An extraordinary Congress at Basel on 24-25 November 1912, held during the First Balkan War, issued a manifesto against war. It warned governments that war could bring revolution.
notes.tip: Examiners ask for the founding (Paris 1889, Brussels bureau), the SPD's strength, and Stuttgart 1907 and Basel 1912. Do not quote the resolutions. Do not confuse revisionism (Bernstein, reform) with revolutionary Marxism.

notes.h: The Second International: collapse in August 1914
notes.b: The International's pledges to stop war were put to the test in the last days of July 1914. They failed, and the failure is the most examined part of its story.
points: The International Socialist Bureau met in Brussels on 29-30 July 1914, and Jaurès spoke there. He was shot dead in a Paris café by a nationalist, Raoul Villain, on 31 July 1914, which removed the leading French advocate of a general strike.

On 4 August 1914 the SPD Reichstag group voted for war credits (money for the war), in the party truce known as the Burgfrieden. Karl Liebknecht was the only Reichstag deputy to vote against war credits, in December 1914.

In France the union sacrée (sacred union) brought socialists such as Jules Guesde and Marcel Sembat into the government in August 1914. In Britain Labour largely backed the war, and Ramsay MacDonald resigned as leader of the Labour MPs.

It collapsed because nationalism proved stronger than class loyalty. German socialists feared repression and Tsarist Russia, French socialists feared German invasion, and ordinary workers were patriotic themselves. There had also been no agreed plan to stop a war.
Socialists split into those who backed their governments, pacifists, and a revolutionary minority including Luxemburg, Liebknecht and Lenin. This minority opposed it as an imperialist war.

Anti-war socialists met at Zimmerwald in Switzerland (September 1915) and at Kienthal (April 1916). The split helped produce the communist parties and the Third (Communist) International, the Comintern, founded in Moscow in March 1919.
notes.tip: Explaining why nationalism beat internationalism scores higher than describing congresses. Date the war-credits vote 4 August 1914 and say the split helped produce the Comintern. Do not say it led directly to the communist parties.

notes.b: Luxemburg was a Marxist theorist, speaker and journalist on the left of the SPD, a participant in the International's debates and a leading opponent of the war. She was a witness to the SPD's vote of 1914 and to the Russian Revolution.
points: She was born on 5 March 1871 in Zamość, Russian-ruled Poland, into a Jewish family. A childhood hip condition left a limp that did not stop her speaking in public. She studied at the University of Zurich (doctorate 1897).

In 1893 she co-founded the Social Democracy of the Kingdom of Poland (later the SDKPiL), opposing Polish independence as a goal because she put class before nation. In 1898 she moved to Germany, gained citizenship by a marriage of convenience, and joined the SPD on its left.

In Reform or Revolution (1899) she attacked Bernstein's revisionism. She went to Warsaw in December 1905 to join the Russian revolution and was arrested in March 1906. Her pamphlet The Mass Strike, the Party and the Trade Unions (1906) argued for the mass strike as a revolutionary weapon.

She taught at the SPD party school in Berlin (1907-14) and wrote The Accumulation of Capital (1913), an economic theory of imperialism. At the Stuttgart Congress in 1907 she helped amend the anti-war resolution with Lenin and Martov.

For anti-war speeches in 1913 urging workers not to take up arms against other nations she was tried and sentenced to a year in prison in February 1914; she began the sentence in February 1915. The SPD's vote for war credits on 4 August 1914 horrified her.

With Karl Liebknecht, Franz Mehring and Clara Zetkin she formed the International group (1915), which became the Spartacus group (1916). In prison from February 1915 to February 1916, and again from July 1916 in 'protective custody' until November 1918, she wrote the Junius pamphlet (1915, published 1916), condemning the war.

She welcomed the Russian Revolution of 1917 but criticised Bolshevik dictatorship and the closing the Constituent Assembly: 'Freedom is always the freedom of the one who thinks differently.' She co-founded the KPD (30 December 1918-1 January 1919), thought the January 1919 rising premature but backed it once begun.

Freikorps soldiers murdered her and Liebknecht in Berlin on 15 January 1919 and threw her body in the Landwehr Canal. To the SPD leaders and conservatives she was a dangerous agitator, and enemies called her 'Red Rosa'; supporters saw a courageous internationalist, Lenin's praise was mixed. Historians admire a major Marxist thinker who opposed both militarism and dictatorship, but debate her practicality.
notes.tip: Give her career in order with dates: birth, Poland, Germany 1898, Reform or Revolution, 1905, The Accumulation of Capital, anti-war sentence, Spartacists, Junius pamphlet, prison, KPD, murder. Marks also go to her significance: consistent opposition to war and criticism of Bolshevik methods. Do not say she opposed the rising without qualification.

notes.h: Causes of the First World War: long-term and short-term
notes.b: The war had no single cause. Long-term pressures made Europe dangerous, and a chain of Balkan events from 1908 to 1914 set them off.
points: Alliances: Europe was divided into the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente, so a local quarrel could bring in all the Great Powers.
Militarism and war plans: the powers built large conscript armies and had mobilisation timetables that left little time for diplomacy. The Schlieffen Plan required a swift attack on France.
Naval and colonial rivalry: the Anglo-German naval race and the Moroccan crises poisoned relations between the powers.

Nationalism: South Slav nationalism threatened Austria-Hungary, French revanche (revenge) aimed to recover Alsace-Lorraine, which Germany annexed in 1871, and pan-Slavism and pan-Germanism pushed Russia and Germany towards confrontation.

Short-term causes were the Bosnian crisis (1908-09), the Balkan Wars, the assassination at Sarajevo, the blank cheque, the ultimatum, the mobilisations and Belgium. Each made the next crisis more dangerous.
The Balkans were where Austrian and Russian interests met. Neither could back down without losing Great Power status, which is why a regional quarrel could not be left alone.
notes.tip: Examiners reward a judgement that there was no single cause, with long-term causes linked to the Balkan trigger and the July crisis in date order. In a question on international tensions, the Austro-Russian rivalry is one strand among Franco-German hostility, the blocs and the naval race.

notes.h: The role of each power in July 1914
notes.b: Each government acted out of a fear as well as an aim. Pairing what each did with what it feared shows why none backed down.
points: Austria-Hungary issued the ultimatum and declared war on Serbia because it feared that Slav nationalism would break up the empire and cost it Great Power status.
Germany gave the blank cheque and hoped for a short, localised war. It feared encirclement, and the Schlieffen Plan meant it could not wait once Russia mobilised.
Russia backed Serbia and mobilised, because it feared losing prestige and status after the humiliation of 1909.
France reaffirmed support for Russia in the visit of 20-23 July and mobilised, because it feared a German attack and wanted to keep its ally.
Britain declared war on 4 August after the invasion of Belgium, because it was concerned for the balance of power and had the Entente with France.
Serbia accepted most of the ultimatum but refused Austrian officials on its soil, because it feared losing its sovereignty. It had begun mobilising on 25 July.

notes.b: Who started the First World War has been argued over since 1914. Examiners reward paired views and a reasoned conclusion, not a one-sided verdict.
points: Contemporary German view: Germany was encircled and forced into a defensive war by Russian mobilisation. Entente view: Germany and Austria-Hungary were aggressors (blank cheque, ultimatum, Belgium). This fed the war-guilt clause, Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles (1919).
Interwar view: David Lloyd George, in his War Memoirs, said the nations 'slithered over the brink' into war. This suggests shared responsibility rather than one guilty power.

Fritz Fischer, a German historian, argued in Germany's Aims in the First World War (German edition 1961) that German leaders deliberately risked or sought war for world-power aims. His view raised an enduring debate about German war aims.
Christopher Clark, in The Sleepwalkers: How Europe Went to War in 1914 (2012), argues that all the powers, Serbia included, share responsibility. He stresses contingency and Balkan politics.

Austria-Hungary's decision to crush Serbia, Serbian nationalism, Russian backing of Serbia, German backing of Austria and military planning were all links in the chain. Historians differ on the weight of each, so weigh them.

Could organised workers have stopped the war? On paper the International was strong, as Stuttgart (1907) and Basel (1912) showed. It failed because nationalism was stronger, there was no agreed plan and workers feared repression.

Luxemburg's achievements were her theory, her consistent opposition to war and the founding of the KPD. Her limits were a small following, the failed rising and her murder before she could shape events.
notes.tip: Pair Fischer (German guilt, 1961) against Clark (shared responsibility, 2012) and finish with a reasoned conclusion on how much blame Germany and Austria-Hungary bear. Do not confuse the two.

keyTerms.definition: Loyalty to a nation and the belief that it should be united and self-governing; South Slav nationalism in Serbia and Bosnia threatened Austria-Hungary.
A situation in which no single state can dominate Europe because rivals combine to check it; Britain's entry in 1914 was justified by this principle and the neutrality of Belgium.
The federation of socialist and labour parties founded in Paris in 1889, which passed anti-war resolutions but collapsed in August 1914.
The Serbian officers' secret society, Unification or Death, founded in 1911 and led by Apis, which supported the Bosnian conspirators.
The movement of young Bosnian Serb and South Slav nationalists, to which Gavrilo Princip belonged, who wanted to end Habsburg rule.
Germany's unconditional promise of support to Austria-Hungary on 5-6 July 1914.
The German plan to defeat France quickly by attacking through Belgium, before turning against Russia.
The summoning and deployment of an army for war; in 1914 the timetable of mobilisations left little time for diplomacy.
The revolutionary socialist group formed in 1916 by Luxemburg and Liebknecht to oppose the war; it became the core of the German Communist Party.

factCards.definition: At the Congress of Berlin in 1878, which recognised it as independent of the Ottoman Empire.

factCards.term: What happened in Belgrade in June 1903?
factCards.definition: Army officers murdered King Alexander and Queen Draga; Peter I of the Karadjordjević dynasty took the throne and Serbia turned towards Russia.
From 1906 Austria-Hungary closed its market to Serbian livestock; Serbia found new markets and Austrian influence declined.

factCards.term: Bosnian crisis: when and who was humiliated?
factCards.definition: Austria annexed Bosnia in October 1908; Germany forced Russia and Serbia to accept it in March 1909.
Serbia doubled in size and gained Macedonia and Kosovo (Treaty of Bucharest, 1913) but was denied an Adriatic port by the creation of Albania.
Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević, head of Serbian military intelligence and leader of the Black Hand.

factCards.term: Who assassinated Franz Ferdinand, and when?
factCards.definition: Gavrilo Princip, a 19-year-old Bosnian Serb of Young Bosnia, in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914.
An Austro-Hungarian note of 23 July with ten demands and a 48-hour deadline, deliberately made hard to accept.

factCards.term: July crisis in dates: declarations of war
factCards.definition: Austria on Serbia 28 July; Germany on Russia 1 August and France 3 August; Britain on Germany 4 August after the invasion of Belgium.

factCards.term: Why did Britain enter the war?
factCards.definition: German invasion of Belgium, whose neutrality Britain had guaranteed by the Treaty of London of 1839, and concern for the balance of power.
Founded Paris 1889; Stuttgart 1907 and Basel 1912 passed anti-war resolutions; it collapsed in August 1914.
The French socialist leader and campaigner against war was assassinated by a nationalist on 31 July 1914.
Born 1871 in Zamość; Junius pamphlet (1915); Spartacus League; helped found the KPD; murdered by Freikorps on 15 January 1919.

factCards.term: How do Fischer and Clark differ on 1914?
factCards.definition: Fischer (1961) blamed German leaders for deliberately risking war; Clark (2012) saw all the powers as sleepwalkers sharing responsibility.
